title: Nix Evaluation Is a Scheduling Problem
excerpt: Why I built Evix, and my ramblings on Nix evaluation
content_html:
Most, if not all, Nix tools I build (or at least, consider building) eventually want to do one little, very boring thing. They want a list of derivations an expression produces, and well, they need to find a way to get it. Not necessarily a build log—I’ve got a crate for that already and those are relatively trivial to parse already and not a closure but a list of jobs. Those usually require their attribute paths, names, systems, .drv paths and outputs to be visible and if you’re building something like Hydra then you need those before you can decide what to build, i.e., those are the things a CI system needs before it can decide what changed. While I haven’t quite tried, those are also things I imagine a deployment tool needs before it can decide whether the graph in front of it is the same abomination or/and deployment abstraction it saw five minutes ago.

This isn’t exactly a problem statement, but it’s more or less the problem I’ve had. Because it sounds like a one-time cost, however, you eventually realize that it isn’t. You also realize that it’s about the inner loop. If you don’t realize what it’s about, then you make the same mistake I did and think to yourself about how TRULY intelligent you are and how you could totally, DEFINITELY get away with re-using the same hacks over and over again.

I think the first time I’ve used this model was in my NixOS configuration’s CI where I combined nix-eval-jobs with jq and then passed the graph to Nix to build my things. Important distinction here is that a CI system asks on every push. A fleet of nixosConfigurations asks once per host, then again when you only care about one system, then again when you want a proper diff. A watcher asks after each file write. A daemon asks because a separate command invocation forgot what the previous one already learned. And evaluating a real flake is not free either. It is thousands of attributes, lazy thunks waking up (just enough to hurt you), and a wall-clock cost you notice mostly because you pay it again for the next question. Now let me state the obvious: Nix’s eval cache sucks. And I can tell you that I am not interested in a cache-shaped thing that’s masquerading as one. Although Evix fixes that too. Just because.

For a very long time I’ve thought that my complaint was that evaluation was slow (it is) and that the output was annoying to parse (it is). It’s roughly the same kind of experience as having an entire piano fall on top of your head while taking a nice little evening stroll but that’s not what ruins my day. What annoys me the most is not having a gravitationally-challenged piano deciding to ruin my evening stroll but the cost that is the program doing the evaluation had already built the interesting structure, printed a representation of it, and then died. Naturally the graph dies with it. Go figure.

When I started calling jq (which I’m not a huge fan of) I slowly started to grow suspicious that the tool I’m using is… wrong. As I’ve mentioned, I initially started by slapping nix-eval-jobs on top of my problems and I do not want to lead you to think it is bad software, 1 but it’s pretty much not what I was looking for. There were still a lot of annoying gaps that would take too long to fill via traditional means and I know it’d suck to do so because C++ sucks. Anyway, my point is that it’s a relatively good tool for finding what a Nix job evaluator should find and Evix still leans on it in benchmarks because I acknowledge it, and I strive to create something better than it.

Enter, Evix

Evix is what I wrote to solve my general woes around structured and persistent evaluations. It is a library-first async Nix evaluation engine that evaluates flakes, files or inline expressions through the stable Nix C API, via my very own nix-bindings, and reports derivations as typed events. There exists a CLI too, in case you want to replace nix-eval-jobs in your CI setups, but despite being very useful it is not the center of my design. The center is the embeddable library API and Session: a long-lived evaluation object that can stream the first run, retain the graph, answer queries, compute diffs, and watch local inputs for changes. The daemon is complementary, and it is ultimately just that idea moved behind a Unix socket so separate command invocations can share a warm session instead of re-enacting the fall of man every time you type a new command.

As much as I want to replace Nix, Evix is not a Nix replacement and I don’t replace Nix yet. Evix is, most simply put, the architecture around evaluation: process isolation, scheduling, backpressure, event accumulation, daemon state, remote workers, and enough respect for the C API that I do not have to scrape a terminal and call it data or torture myself with the C++ API. If there is a technical marvel here, it is not that I discovered fire. No, I was not there to discover fire (I’m not that old) but the parts of Evix are quite interesting nevertheless. Most of them mundane and sharp-edged, line up into a proper model where Nix evaluation becomes something more reliable and something you can pretty much hold on to—for the lack of a better term.

One Value, One Event

If you’re not bored with me yet, I’d like to describe the model to you. Maybe you’ll find it interesting, or maybe you’ve got better ideas than me and you’ll help develop mine. In either case, I would like to spend the rest of this post talking about how Evix operates.

The model starts smaller than what you might expect. A worker does not walk a whole flake as most tools often do as I’ve come to observe. It evaluates one attribute path and returns one event. Hand it packages.x86_64-linux.hello and it navigates from the root value to that path through the Nix C API, auto-calling functions on the way when the configured arguments make that possible. Then it asks what it found. If the value is a derivation, Evix reads the derivation name, target system, .drv path and outputs. If requested, it also reads meta, input derivations from the .drv, Hydra-style constituents, and registers GC roots. If the value is an attribute set, Evix does not recursively disappear into it. It returns the child names as an event. If forcing the value throws, that is an error event. Nonfatal errors are part of the stream, not a reason to throw away the whole run.

That last sentence is more important than it looks. A large Nix graph is not a Victorian—or 19th century Ottoman—novel where every character has to survive until the last chapter. One bad package should not erase the packages next to it. Errors need names and paths and enough structure that a caller (and consequently, you) can decide what to do with them. A byte stream can tell you something went wrong. A typed event can tell you where it went wrong and still let the rest of the graph arrive. Everybody wins!

It helps to see the thing Evix is walking. A flake output is usually a tree of attribute sets with derivations at the leaves, trimmed down to something like this:

.#                       root; always recursed into
├─ packages
│  ├─ x86_64-linux       attrset    (expand: one work item per child)
│  │  ├─ hello           derivation (leaf)  hello-2.12.1
│  │  ├─ git             derivation (leaf)  git-2.45.2
│  │  └─ ripgrep         derivation (leaf)  ripgrep-14.1.0
│  └─ aarch64-linux      attrset
│     ├─ hello           derivation (leaf)
│     └─ firefox         derivation (leaf)
└─ devShells
   └─ x86_64-linux
      └─ default         derivation (leaf)

Behold my artistic skills! The recursion does not live inside a call stack that one worker owns. It lives in a queue. The coordinator seeds the queue with the root path. A worker pulls a path, evaluates it, and returns an event. An attrset event adds more paths to the queue. A derivation event is terminal. An error event is terminal for that path. The run ends when the queue is empty and no worker is busy.

Walked as a queue rather than a private recursion, that tree drains roughly like this, in whatever order the workers happen to answer:

queue: [ .# ]
  .#                            attrset    -> enqueue packages, devShells
  packages                      attrset    -> enqueue packages.x86_64-linux, ...
  packages.x86_64-linux         attrset    -> enqueue ...hello, ...git, ...ripgrep
  packages.x86_64-linux.hello   derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing
  packages.x86_64-linux.git     derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing
  ...
empty queue, nothing in flight  -> we're done

[!NOTE] Evix does not recurse into every attrset by default. It follows the same basic idea tools like this usually follow: recurse at the root, and recurse into attrsets that opt in with recurseForDerivations. There is a --force-recurse option for the times you really do want to kick down every door, but the default is less stupid. Nixpkgs has many rooms. Some contain jobs. Some contain machinery. Some contain things that make you regret curiosity as a concept and think about the poor cats.

The important invariant, which I call important because it caused many breakages and a lot of pain, is that the answer is a graph keyed by attribute path, not by the order events happened to arrive. One worker and four workers should produce the same graph. Naturally, local workers and remote workers should feed the same accumulator. The event stream is temporal because programs live in time, but the resulting graph is not supposed to depend on scheduler luck. That is the licence to use parallelism. 2

It’s also worth talking about Evix’s benchmark suite. I’m yet to benchmark Evix in more advanced production scenarios, but on the current toy3 benchmark fixture, which is designed to measure scheduling and evaluation overhead rather than build time, Evix with one local worker sits around 318ms, four local workers around 198ms, and eight local workers around 216ms. nix-eval-jobs with four workers is around 359ms on the same fixture. Remote-only evaluation over loopback with four workers lands around 269ms. 4 Do not read those numbers as a universal law. The fixture is rather cheap, so overheads are loud and real flakes will move the constants around. Read them as evidence that the session, graph and distribution model are not bought with a throughput tax large enough to make the project silly.

Processes, Not Threads

If you have ever watched a Nix evaluation climb past the memory you have and get killed three-quarters of the way through, taking the whole run with it, this is the part that concerns you. 5 Evix workers are subprocesses, not threads. The host process owns the queue and the warm graph. Each worker owns its Nix context, store handle, eval state and root value. The boundary is crude in the way Unix is crude, which is to say it is one of the few crude things in computing that still works. I also have some few crass things to say about it all.

After each attribute, the worker checks its maximum resident set size against a configured limit, 4 GB by default. If the worker is over the line, it returns a Restart status and exits. The coordinator goes ahead and spawns a fresh worker and continues feeding the same queue. The graph is in the parent, so the graph survives. The worker’s heap is in the worker, so the leak does not become some kind of a blood oath the host process has to honor forever. This is especially important if you’re interested in embedding. By default, local workers re-exec the embedding binary and enter the worker protocol when EVIX_WORKER is set. If your host program cannot or should not re-exec itself, you can point ConfigBuilder::worker_exe at a dedicated worker executable instead. The worker protocol is still the same: setup message, work path, event, status. The magic is mostly refusing to make the embedding process also be the place where libnix gets to leak memory for sport.

One footnote worth keeping around before I wrap up this section is that the memory check happens between attributes. It catches the common case where a worker grows over many paths, BUT, it does not save you from one attribute that detonates mid-force before control returns to the check. Evix can time out an item, abort a worker and reconnect. It can report stderr. It can keep the host alive. It cannot make libnix interruption into a property it does not have. I’m a poor man. All I’ve got is a process boundary and an RSS check. Different budgets, I guess.

The Session Is The Product

The first version of the idea that evolved to the Evix of today could be explained roughly as “evaluate once, keep the graph.” That is, well, still true, but the current model is more precise: an evaluation configuration opens a Session; the session streams the initial event log once; draining that stream populates warm state; queries and diffs operate on that warm state until you replace it. This sounds like API trivia, which I’d love to provide, but it is genuinely important because it basically changes the shape of the programs you can write. A CLI pipeline gives you a list. A session gives you memory and identity. The graph is a HashMap keyed by attribute path, with derivation records as values. A query is a filter over that graph: systems, attribute prefixes, exact attrs, names, .drv paths, include patterns, exclude patterns. A diff is a fresh evaluation compared with the previous graph; if the same attribute path points to a different .drv path, Evix treats it as a remove and an add. Something something the ship of Theseus something.

The library API exposes that more directly. Session::stream is single-use because the initial evaluation is single-use. Session::query_snapshot reads the warm graph. Session::diff_once re-evaluates and swaps in the new graph. Session::watch does the same lil’ dance after fs notifications for local files and local flake inputs. The bounded variants exist because embedders sometimes need backpressure, as one does, and unbounded channels are a nice way to turn “my stdout is slow” into “honey, why is my process enormous?” Ask me how I know. Actually, please don’t.

The Daemon(host)

The daemon is a thin extension of the same idea as Evix. It listens on a Unix socket, keeps a small registry of warm sessions, and keys them by the evaluation config: input, arguments, Nix options, worker count, memory limit, remote endpoints, metadata flags, the whole boring lot. It’s also primed to do a lot more.

Actually the idea for the daemon comes from our goals in Circus to distribute not only builds, but evaluation as well. A cache that ignores the configuration is not a cache, it is a liar with good latency. If you evaluated with one set of overrides and query with another, you should get a miss, not a beautifully fast wrong answer. Similarly, a cache is not a proper cache if it’s not a cache according to a different machine.

Alongside the daemon, there exist a few other evix commands to wrap Evix’s excellent (if I may say so myself) library interface:

  • evix eval evaluates once and streams NDJSON. If the daemon is available, it can also leave a warm session behind.
  • evix query asks an already warm daemon session for a filtered snapshot.
  • evix diff re-evaluates and compares against the warm graph.
  • evix watch evaluates a local file or flake and emits diffs as watched inputs change.
  • evix worker starts a remote worker service.
  • evix daemon starts the Unix-socket daemon explicitly, if you do not want the CLI to pretend all of this happens by divine intervention.

So my point is that Evix is not merely a faster way to print the same list. It is a way to keep the evaluated graph resident long enough that follow-up questions become ordinary program operations. It also isn’t a Nix eval wrapper. Evix was specifically designed for Circus, the (hopefully futureproof) CI I am working on at Manic Systems, where the difference between “wait for evaluation” and “ask the already evaluated world what changed” is critical for our use case. The latter is a much nicer sentence to live inside—it’s also a nicer way of doing what Hydra does, and more reliable too.

Workers That Aren’t Here (They Are On Strike)

A worker is an odd little thing that I decided to mirror from Circus’ distributed agents design/concept where a worker receives an attribute path and returns an event. Once you phrase it that way, there is no deep reason it has to be on the same machine as the coordinator—similar to Circus’ agents. This is where Evix stops being a local optimization and starts looking like a scheduler in the old-fashioned sense. It has a queue, and opinions about who should do what. Remote workers are TCP services speaking Cap’n Proto messages. Remember when I said distributed evaluation? Yeah that’s exactly it.

A connection opens with a setup handshake containing the evaluation config, protocol version, token, and expected store directory. Then it repeats the small loop: Work(path) goes out, Event and Status come back. TCP_NODELAY is set because the protocol is one tiny request-response per attribute, and Nagle’s algorithm is what happens when the network stack decides your latency profile should be a moral lesson. 6

Each remote connection gets its own evaluator subprocess on the far end, so --remote builder-a:7357 x86_64-linux 4 means four worker connections to that endpoint. With --workers 0 and at least one remote, the coordinator can run no local workers at all. At that point your local process is almost pure scheduler: it owns the queue and graph, while the machines that can actually evaluate the interesting systems do the forcing. On this note, however, system routing has a subtle limitation: a derivation’s system is not known until the attribute has been evaluated. Evix therefore cannot always know, before evaluation, which machine is the perfect one for a path. Remotes declare the systems they own, and the coordinator checks returned derivations against the pool. If some local, catch-all, or owning remote accepts that system, the event is valid. If no worker in the pool accepts it, evaluation fails by name with a fatal error instead of quietly losing the derivation. That is less magical than perfect pre-routing and much better than lying to ourselves or making a best-effort guess.

There is also a store-directory handshake. A remote whose Nix store directory does not match the coordinator’s is rejected, because .drv and output paths are only meaningful to the consumer if they point into the same kind of store. This is, well, not remote building. Obviously. Evix is not copying build products around. It is evaluating and reporting derivations. If you want remote build output transfer, that belongs to Nix’s builder model or to a CI system above evix, not to the evaluator pretending it also wants to be a builder when it grows up. Quite frankly this is the part of Evix I like most, because it is not grand. It does not say “distributed systems” and then demand a control plane, a service mesh, and worse… YAML. It says the unit of work is already serializable, the event is already serializable, and a worker was already disposable. Put a socket between them. Make the protocol explicit. Refuse remotes that cannot mean the same store paths. Move on.

Talking To Nix Without Bespoke Bash

Earlier in this post I’ve mentioned using Nix (and friends) in CI. If you don’t remember this, it’s fine—I’m aware I’ve been yapping for too long. Long story short, this entire endeavour—as expected from all the context and pain surrounding GHA— was done using Bash. Which is to say that it’s typically not too easy to perform Nix evaluations without calling nix eval or the C++ APIs. This is where I want to mention the other, “quiet” part of Evix. As mentioned earlier, Evix talks to Nix through the C API. This was not done for aesthetic purity, although I do enjoy not parsing human-facing text (or using C++) like an animal. It was done because an embedding library needs typed boundaries.

An input is one of three things:

  1. a flake reference,
  2. a Nix file, or
  3. an inline expression.

Auto-call arguments can be expressions or strings. Flake inputs can be overridden while locking. Nix options can be passed through to the worker environment before the worker opens the store or builds its eval state. Flake locking is handled before workers start, and the locked graph is imported inside workers so multi-worker evaluation is not each process inventing its own answer to what the flake meant at that moment. Local path flakes are checked against their flake.lock; non-local refs are still a place where reproducibility needs care, because reality remains rude.

The output is typed first and JSON later. The Rust enum has variants for derivations, attrsets and errors. The CLI flattens those into NDJSON because NDJSON is useful and boring, two properties I respect deeply in formats. With --meta, Evix tries to convert meta into freeform JSON and drops nested fields that cannot be forced or represented. With --show-input-drvs, it reads input derivations from the .drv file. Aggregate jobs with constituents carry those too. None of this needs a regex, or plural, regrets.

That is also why the project is not really about the CLI. The CLI is convenient, and I use it, but the library is the point. A Rust service can open a Session, drain the stream, query the warm graph, compute a diff, or run a watcher without shelling out and reconstructing structure from text. If the service is a web backend, Evix can live as a native sidecar or daemon behind whatever HTTP or WebSocket API you actually want. If you want browser WASM, bad news: the current backend is native by design. It links libnix, opens a Nix store, uses Unix subprocesses, and speaks Unix sockets and TCP. An in-browser evaluator would need a different backend, probably one we control entirely. Sad, I know. Alas, that’s what we have. However it’s not the end.

What Evix Solves

The problem Evix solves is not “Nix evaluation exists.” The problem is that serious tools around Nix need evaluation to become a reusable service boundary, and not a ceremony performed by a subprocess every time. For CI specifically, the useful object is a graph that can be diffed between commits. For your fleet of NixOS configurations, it is a graph that can be filtered by system, prefix, name or .drv path. For a watch command, it is a previous graph and a new graph with errors attached to the comparison instead of hidden in a terminal scrollback. For distributed evaluation, it is a queue of independent attribute paths that local and remote workers can pull from without changing what the final graph means. For an embedding application, it is a typed API that does not ask the caller to summon a shell and interpret stdout as ontology. Thus, this I’ve built Evix. Circus needs to evaluate jobsets often, keep them around, ask what changed, and eventually hand builds to the right place. I do not want that CI to spend its life recomputing the same graph because the previous process threw away the one thing I cared about. I do not want an aarch64 board to be represented by an x86_64 laptop. I do not want one broken package to make the rest of the job graph unknowable. I do not want the evaluator and the builder to become one swollen process just because both words appear near each other in a README. Yada yada. My point is that Evix draws the line where I needed it. Evaluation discovers derivations. Building is somebody else’s problem, usually Nix itself or Circus. Building is stateful, resource-hungry, cache-sensitive, failure-prone in completely different ways, and full of policy. Evaluation is already enough of a problem, and I have 99 problems. Evaluation is 99 of them.

Where It Stops

Evix is rather young, and there are real ceilings. If you end up trying Evix and get rather disappointed, I ask that you attribute to its lack of maturity. I’ve recently released 2.0.0 to revise its model in its entirety and it was a much larger refactor than I feel I was equipped to deal with. Still, it turned out quite well and Circus’ own CI test suite is now green across the board. That said, I’ll be remiss if I don’t mention the issues such as that a worker can still die inside one awful force. Remote workers need compatible stores and trusted networking; expose the TCP service over a tunnel or VPN, not to the entire internet like you are trying to speedrun regret. System routing is also rather constrained by the fact that the system is discovered after evaluation—rather unsurprisingly. The daemon keeps warm sessions, but it is not a distributed database and should not be asked to cosplay as one. THOUGH, it may be possible in the future. Last but not least, remember that the C API is stable enough to build on, but Nix is still Nix, with all the fun that implies and several other kinds of fun it invents at runtime.

There are also things Evix intentionally does not do. One big example is building. I’ve considered giving it a component like evix build, but compared to the surface of evaluation, building is truly a different kind of monster. To let Evix also do building, I would be required to solve several problems that are not even remotely addressed in flakes, and I do not have the patience for that can of worms yet—no, I’m not a patient man.

It does not solve binary cache policy. It does not make remote flakes locally watchable when there is no local path to subscribe to. It does not turn a Nix graph into a web frontend by itself. It will tell you what derivations exist, what paths they would produce, what inputs they mention if you ask, and how a later evaluation differs from an earlier one. That is the promise. A narrow promise, but a useful one. I do not expect Evix to be groundbreaking, but I expect it to be useful. It’s got a lot of potential, and thus my dear reader, I invite you to harness it. Come talk to me, let me know what you need even.

Closing Thoughts

So, that is Evix as it stands today. It’s certainly been through a lot of iterations over I can probably only describe as ages before I decided to sit down and port my low-effort Python/Bash/C++ bullshit to proper Rust. It is not a one-shot evaluator (anymore) with a nicer coat of paint, but a session-oriented evaluation engine with a proper CLI attached. The combination changes the question from “how do I print the jobs again?” to “what do I want to ask the graph I already have?” If you’re building with Evix it gives you a very nice toolkit to answer your questions in mere seconds. That’s about it for what my “trick” is. I want to go ahead, get a bit philosophical, and say that a tool is partly defined by what it lets you remember. The old shape made evaluation an event. Evix, however, tries to make it an object: scheduled, isolated, queryable, diffable, and capable of crossing machine boundaries without pretending those boundaries are not there.

If a one-shot list piped into jq is all you need, or rather, insist is all you need then you do not need any of this. But by all means, use the simpler thing and enjoy the rare luxury of not needing my problems. I needed evaluation to stay alive inside a program, with typed values instead of a byte stream, and with enough scheduling machinery that the work could survive large graphs, leaky workers and machines that are not the one under my hands. That is a narrow need, and it is mine.

Evix is on GitHub if that sounds like your problem too. Cheers.

It is a library-first async Nix evaluation engine that evaluates flakes, files or inline expressions through the stable Nix C API, via my very own nix-bindings, and reports derivations as typed events. There exists a CLI too, in case you want to replace nix-eval-jobs in your CI setups, but despite being very useful it is not the center of my design. The center is the embeddable library API and Session: a long-lived evaluation object that can stream the first run, retain the graph, answer queries, compute diffs, and watch local inputs for changes. The daemon is complementary, and it is ultimately just that idea moved behind a Unix socket so separate command invocations can share a warm session instead of re-enacting the fall of man every time you type a new command. As much as I want to replace Nix, Evix is not a Nix replacement and I don’t replace Nix yet. Evix is, most simply put, the architecture around evaluation: process isolation, scheduling, backpressure, event accumulation, daemon state, remote workers, and enough respect for the C API that I do not have to scrape a terminal and call it data or torture myself with the C++ API. If there is a technical marvel here, it is not that I discovered fire. No, I was not there to discover fire (I’m not that old) but the parts of Evix are quite interesting nevertheless. Most of them mundane and sharp-edged, line up into a proper model where Nix evaluation becomes something more reliable and something you can pretty much hold on to—for the lack of a better term. One Value, One Event If you’re not bored with me yet, I’d like to describe the model to you. Maybe you’ll find it interesting, or maybe you’ve got better ideas than me and you’ll help develop mine. In either case, I would like to spend the rest of this post talking about how Evix operates. The model starts smaller than what you might expect. A worker does not walk a whole flake as most tools often do as I’ve come to observe. It evaluates one attribute path and returns one event. Hand it packages.x86_64-linux.hello and it navigates from the root value to that path through the Nix C API, auto-calling functions on the way when the configured arguments make that possible. Then it asks what it found. If the value is a derivation, Evix reads the derivation name, target system, .drv path and outputs. If requested, it also reads meta, input derivations from the .drv, Hydra-style constituents, and registers GC roots. If the value is an attribute set, Evix does not recursively disappear into it. It returns the child names as an event. If forcing the value throws, that is an error event. Nonfatal errors are part of the stream, not a reason to throw away the whole run. That last sentence is more important than it looks. A large Nix graph is not a Victorian—or 19th century Ottoman—novel where every character has to survive until the last chapter. One bad package should not erase the packages next to it. Errors need names and paths and enough structure that a caller (and consequently, you) can decide what to do with them. A byte stream can tell you something went wrong. A typed event can tell you where it went wrong and still let the rest of the graph arrive. Everybody wins! It helps to see the thing Evix is walking. A flake output is usually a tree of attribute sets with derivations at the leaves, trimmed down to something like this: .# root; always recursed into├─ packages│ ├─ x86_64-linux attrset (expand: one work item per child)│ │ ├─ hello derivation (leaf) hello-2.12.1│ │ ├─ git derivation (leaf) git-2.45.2│ │ └─ ripgrep derivation (leaf) ripgrep-14.1.0│ └─ aarch64-linux attrset│ ├─ hello derivation (leaf)│ └─ firefox derivation (leaf)└─ devShells └─ x86_64-linux └─ default derivation (leaf) Behold my artistic skills! The recursion does not live inside a call stack that one worker owns. It lives in a queue. The coordinator seeds the queue with the root path. A worker pulls a path, evaluates it, and returns an event. An attrset event adds more paths to the queue. A derivation event is terminal. An error event is terminal for that path. The run ends when the queue is empty and no worker is busy. Walked as a queue rather than a private recursion, that tree drains roughly like this, in whatever order the workers happen to answer: queue: [ .# ] .# attrset -> enqueue packages, devShells packages attrset -> enqueue packages.x86_64-linux, ... packages.x86_64-linux attrset -> enqueue ...hello, ...git, ...ripgrep packages.x86_64-linux.hello derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing packages.x86_64-linux.git derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing ...empty queue, nothing in flight -> we're done [!NOTE] Evix does not recurse into every attrset by default. It follows the same basic idea tools like this usually follow: recurse at the root, and recurse into attrsets that opt in with recurseForDerivations. There is a --force-recurse option for the times you really do want to kick down every door, but the default is less stupid. Nixpkgs has many rooms. Some contain jobs. Some contain machinery. Some contain things that make you regret curiosity as a concept and think about the poor cats. The important invariant, which I call important because it caused many breakages and a lot of pain, is that the answer is a graph keyed by attribute path, not by the order events happened to arrive. One worker and four workers should produce the same graph. Naturally, local workers and remote workers should feed the same accumulator. The event stream is temporal because programs live in time, but the resulting graph is not supposed to depend on scheduler luck. That is the licence to use parallelism. 2 It’s also worth talking about Evix’s benchmark suite. I’m yet to benchmark Evix in more advanced production scenarios, but on the current toy3 benchmark fixture, which is designed to measure scheduling and evaluation overhead rather than build time, Evix with one local worker sits around 318ms, four local workers around 198ms, and eight local workers around 216ms. nix-eval-jobs with four workers is around 359ms on the same fixture. Remote-only evaluation over loopback with four workers lands around 269ms. 4 Do not read those numbers as a universal law. The fixture is rather cheap, so overheads are loud and real flakes will move the constants around. Read them as evidence that the session, graph and distribution model are not bought with a throughput tax large enough to make the project silly. Processes, Not Threads If you have ever watched a Nix evaluation climb past the memory you have and get killed three-quarters of the way through, taking the whole run with it, this is the part that concerns you. 5 Evix workers are subprocesses, not threads. The host process owns the queue and the warm graph. Each worker owns its Nix context, store handle, eval state and root value. The boundary is crude in the way Unix is crude, which is to say it is one of the few crude things in computing that still works. I also have some few crass things to say about it all. After each attribute, the worker checks its maximum resident set size against a configured limit, 4 GB by default. If the worker is over the line, it returns a Restart status and exits. The coordinator goes ahead and spawns a fresh worker and continues feeding the same queue. The graph is in the parent, so the graph survives. The worker’s heap is in the worker, so the leak does not become some kind of a blood oath the host process has to honor forever. This is especially important if you’re interested in embedding. By default, local workers re-exec the embedding binary and enter the worker protocol when EVIX_WORKER is set. If your host program cannot or should not re-exec itself, you can point ConfigBuilder::worker_exe at a dedicated worker executable instead. The worker protocol is still the same: setup message, work path, event, status. The magic is mostly refusing to make the embedding process also be the place where libnix gets to leak memory for sport. One footnote worth keeping around before I wrap up this section is that the memory check happens between attributes. It catches the common case where a worker grows over many paths, BUT, it does not save you from one attribute that detonates mid-force before control returns to the check. Evix can time out an item, abort a worker and reconnect. It can report stderr. It can keep the host alive. It cannot make libnix interruption into a property it does not have. I’m a poor man. All I’ve got is a process boundary and an RSS check. Different budgets, I guess. The Session Is The Product The first version of the idea that evolved to the Evix of today could be explained roughly as “evaluate once, keep the graph.” That is, well, still true, but the current model is more precise: an evaluation configuration opens a Session; the session streams the initial event log once; draining that stream populates warm state; queries and diffs operate on that warm state until you replace it. This sounds like API trivia, which I’d love to provide, but it is genuinely important because it basically changes the shape of the programs you can write. A CLI pipeline gives you a list. A session gives you memory and identity. The graph is a HashMap keyed by attribute path, with derivation records as values. A query is a filter over that graph: systems, attribute prefixes, exact attrs, names, .drv paths, include patterns, exclude patterns. A diff is a fresh evaluation compared with the previous graph; if the same attribute path points to a different .drv path, Evix treats it as a remove and an add. Something something the ship of Theseus something. The library API exposes that more directly. Session::stream is single-use because the initial evaluation is single-use. Session::query_snapshot reads the warm graph. Session::diff_once re-evaluates and swaps in the new graph. Session::watch does the same lil’ dance after fs notifications for local files and local flake inputs. The bounded variants exist because embedders sometimes need backpressure, as one does, and unbounded channels are a nice way to turn “my stdout is slow” into “honey, why is my process enormous?” Ask me how I know. Actually, please don’t. The Daemon(host) The daemon is a thin extension of the same idea as Evix. It listens on a Unix socket, keeps a small registry of warm sessions, and keys them by the evaluation config: input, arguments, Nix options, worker count, memory limit, remote endpoints, metadata flags, the whole boring lot. It’s also primed to do a lot more. Actually the idea for the daemon comes from our goals in Circus to distribute not only builds, but evaluation as well. A cache that ignores the configuration is not a cache, it is a liar with good latency. If you evaluated with one set of overrides and query with another, you should get a miss, not a beautifully fast wrong answer. Similarly, a cache is not a proper cache if it’s not a cache according to a different machine. Alongside the daemon, there exist a few other evix commands to wrap Evix’s excellent (if I may say so myself) library interface: evix eval evaluates once and streams NDJSON. If the daemon is available, it can also leave a warm session behind. evix query asks an already warm daemon session for a filtered snapshot. evix diff re-evaluates and compares against the warm graph. evix watch evaluates a local file or flake and emits diffs as watched inputs change. evix worker starts a remote worker service. evix daemon starts the Unix-socket daemon explicitly, if you do not want the CLI to pretend all of this happens by divine intervention. So my point is that Evix is not merely a faster way to print the same list. It is a way to keep the evaluated graph resident long enough that follow-up questions become ordinary program operations. It also isn’t a Nix eval wrapper. Evix was specifically designed for Circus, the (hopefully futureproof) CI I am working on at Manic Systems, where the difference between “wait for evaluation” and “ask the already evaluated world what changed” is critical for our use case. The latter is a much nicer sentence to live inside—it’s also a nicer way of doing what Hydra does, and more reliable too. Workers That Aren’t Here (They Are On Strike) A worker is an odd little thing that I decided to mirror from Circus’ distributed agents design/concept where a worker receives an attribute path and returns an event. Once you phrase it that way, there is no deep reason it has to be on the same machine as the coordinator—similar to Circus’ agents. This is where Evix stops being a local optimization and starts looking like a scheduler in the old-fashioned sense. It has a queue, and opinions about who should do what. Remote workers are TCP services speaking Cap’n Proto messages. Remember when I said distributed evaluation? Yeah that’s exactly it. A connection opens with a setup handshake containing the evaluation config, protocol version, token, and expected store directory. Then it repeats the small loop: Work(path) goes out, Event and Status come back. TCP_NODELAY is set because the protocol is one tiny request-response per attribute, and Nagle’s algorithm is what happens when the network stack decides your latency profile should be a moral lesson. 6 Each remote connection gets its own evaluator subprocess on the far end, so --remote builder-a:7357 x86_64-linux 4 means four worker connections to that endpoint. With --workers 0 and at least one remote, the coordinator can run no local workers at all. At that point your local process is almost pure scheduler: it owns the queue and graph, while the machines that can actually evaluate the interesting systems do the forcing. On this note, however, system routing has a subtle limitation: a derivation’s system is not known until the attribute has been evaluated. Evix therefore cannot always know, before evaluation, which machine is the perfect one for a path. Remotes declare the systems they own, and the coordinator checks returned derivations against the pool. If some local, catch-all, or owning remote accepts that system, the event is valid. If no worker in the pool accepts it, evaluation fails by name with a fatal error instead of quietly losing the derivation. That is less magical than perfect pre-routing and much better than lying to ourselves or making a best-effort guess. There is also a store-directory handshake. A remote whose Nix store directory does not match the coordinator’s is rejected, because .drv and output paths are only meaningful to the consumer if they point into the same kind of store. This is, well, not remote building. Obviously. Evix is not copying build products around. It is evaluating and reporting derivations. If you want remote build output transfer, that belongs to Nix’s builder model or to a CI system above evix, not to the evaluator pretending it also wants to be a builder when it grows up. Quite frankly this is the part of Evix I like most, because it is not grand. It does not say “distributed systems” and then demand a control plane, a service mesh, and worse… YAML. It says the unit of work is already serializable, the event is already serializable, and a worker was already disposable. Put a socket between them. Make the protocol explicit. Refuse remotes that cannot mean the same store paths. Move on. Talking To Nix Without Bespoke Bash Earlier in this post I’ve mentioned using Nix (and friends) in CI. If you don’t remember this, it’s fine—I’m aware I’ve been yapping for too long. Long story short, this entire endeavour—as expected from all the context and pain surrounding GHA— was done using Bash. Which is to say that it’s typically not too easy to perform Nix evaluations without calling nix eval or the C++ APIs. This is where I want to mention the other, “quiet” part of Evix. As mentioned earlier, Evix talks to Nix through the C API. This was not done for aesthetic purity, although I do enjoy not parsing human-facing text (or using C++) like an animal. It was done because an embedding library needs typed boundaries. An input is one of three things: a flake reference, a Nix file, or an inline expression. Auto-call arguments can be expressions or strings. Flake inputs can be overridden while locking. Nix options can be passed through to the worker environment before the worker opens the store or builds its eval state. Flake locking is handled before workers start, and the locked graph is imported inside workers so multi-worker evaluation is not each process inventing its own answer to what the flake meant at that moment. Local path flakes are checked against their flake.lock; non-local refs are still a place where reproducibility needs care, because reality remains rude. The output is typed first and JSON later. The Rust enum has variants for derivations, attrsets and errors. The CLI flattens those into NDJSON because NDJSON is useful and boring, two properties I respect deeply in formats. With --meta, Evix tries to convert meta into freeform JSON and drops nested fields that cannot be forced or represented. With --show-input-drvs, it reads input derivations from the .drv file. Aggregate jobs with constituents carry those too. None of this needs a regex, or plural, regrets. That is also why the project is not really about the CLI. The CLI is convenient, and I use it, but the library is the point. A Rust service can open a Session, drain the stream, query the warm graph, compute a diff, or run a watcher without shelling out and reconstructing structure from text. If the service is a web backend, Evix can live as a native sidecar or daemon behind whatever HTTP or WebSocket API you actually want. If you want browser WASM, bad news: the current backend is native by design. It links libnix, opens a Nix store, uses Unix subprocesses, and speaks Unix sockets and TCP. An in-browser evaluator would need a different backend, probably one we control entirely. Sad, I know. Alas, that’s what we have. However it’s not the end. What Evix Solves The problem Evix solves is not “Nix evaluation exists.” The problem is that serious tools around Nix need evaluation to become a reusable service boundary, and not a ceremony performed by a subprocess every time. For CI specifically, the useful object is a graph that can be diffed between commits. For your fleet of NixOS configurations, it is a graph that can be filtered by system, prefix, name or .drv path. For a watch command, it is a previous graph and a new graph with errors attached to the comparison instead of hidden in a terminal scrollback. For distributed evaluation, it is a queue of independent attribute paths that local and remote workers can pull from without changing what the final graph means. For an embedding application, it is a typed API that does not ask the caller to summon a shell and interpret stdout as ontology. Thus, this I’ve built Evix. Circus needs to evaluate jobsets often, keep them around, ask what changed, and eventually hand builds to the right place. I do not want that CI to spend its life recomputing the same graph because the previous process threw away the one thing I cared about. I do not want an aarch64 board to be represented by an x86_64 laptop. I do not want one broken package to make the rest of the job graph unknowable. I do not want the evaluator and the builder to become one swollen process just because both words appear near each other in a README. Yada yada. My point is that Evix draws the line where I needed it. Evaluation discovers derivations. Building is somebody else’s problem, usually Nix itself or Circus. Building is stateful, resource-hungry, cache-sensitive, failure-prone in completely different ways, and full of policy. Evaluation is already enough of a problem, and I have 99 problems. Evaluation is 99 of them. Where It Stops Evix is rather young, and there are real ceilings. If you end up trying Evix and get rather disappointed, I ask that you attribute to its lack of maturity. I’ve recently released 2.0.0 to revise its model in its entirety and it was a much larger refactor than I feel I was equipped to deal with. Still, it turned out quite well and Circus’ own CI test suite is now green across the board. That said, I’ll be remiss if I don’t mention the issues such as that a worker can still die inside one awful force. Remote workers need compatible stores and trusted networking; expose the TCP service over a tunnel or VPN, not to the entire internet like you are trying to speedrun regret. System routing is also rather constrained by the fact that the system is discovered after evaluation—rather unsurprisingly. The daemon keeps warm sessions, but it is not a distributed database and should not be asked to cosplay as one. THOUGH, it may be possible in the future. Last but not least, remember that the C API is stable enough to build on, but Nix is still Nix, with all the fun that implies and several other kinds of fun it invents at runtime. There are also things Evix intentionally does not do. One big example is building. I’ve considered giving it a component like evix build, but compared to the surface of evaluation, building is truly a different kind of monster. To let Evix also do building, I would be required to solve several problems that are not even remotely addressed in flakes, and I do not have the patience for that can of worms yet—no, I’m not a patient man. It does not solve binary cache policy. It does not make remote flakes locally watchable when there is no local path to subscribe to. It does not turn a Nix graph into a web frontend by itself. It will tell you what derivations exist, what paths they would produce, what inputs they mention if you ask, and how a later evaluation differs from an earlier one. That is the promise. A narrow promise, but a useful one. I do not expect Evix to be groundbreaking, but I expect it to be useful. It’s got a lot of potential, and thus my dear reader, I invite you to harness it. Come talk to me, let me know what you need even. Closing Thoughts So, that is Evix as it stands today. It’s certainly been through a lot of iterations over I can probably only describe as ages before I decided to sit down and port my low-effort Python/Bash/C++ bullshit to proper Rust. It is not a one-shot evaluator (anymore) with a nicer coat of paint, but a session-oriented evaluation engine with a proper CLI attached. The combination changes the question from “how do I print the jobs again?” to “what do I want to ask the graph I already have?” If you’re building with Evix it gives you a very nice toolkit to answer your questions in mere seconds. That’s about it for what my “trick” is. I want to go ahead, get a bit philosophical, and say that a tool is partly defined by what it lets you remember. The old shape made evaluation an event. Evix, however, tries to make it an object: scheduled, isolated, queryable, diffable, and capable of crossing machine boundaries without pretending those boundaries are not there. If a one-shot list piped into jq is all you need, or rather, insist is all you need then you do not need any of this. But by all means, use the simpler thing and enjoy the rare luxury of not needing my problems. I needed evaluation to stay alive inside a program, with typed values instead of a byte stream, and with enough scheduling machinery that the work could survive large graphs, leaky workers and machines that are not the one under my hands. That is a narrow need, and it is mine. Evix is on GitHub if that sounds like your problem too. Cheers. Footnotes I’m pointing out so that you don’t mistakenly think that I’m inherently negative to every project I aim to replace. I do have my reservations about nix-eval-jobs, and some of its development, but it would be too easy to dishonestly tell you Evix is good because nix-eval-jobs is bad and, well, that’s not what I’m interested in doing here. The main difference between the two projects ultimately boils down to the fact that my eyes are on a different boundary. I wish to evaluate, keep the graph, answer typed questions and let work happen on machines that are not necessarily this one. Hope it is clear that this is not me discouraging you to drop nix-eval-jobs because it is bad; this is me telling you why Evix exists and how it operates under different assumptions for an ultimately larger scope. Namely, regarding surrounding my needs. Maybe even yours. ↩ We used to have good things. ↩ Anyone who’s experienced in Nix will be able to tell you that it’s a bad benchmark suite. Admittedly I haven’t thought too much about benchmarking and I probably should test with real-life scenarios sooner than later. ↩ The benchmark fixture is a stinky pile of trivial derivations whose .drv paths are computed but never built. There is no IO-heavy build hiding scheduler overhead. The daemon numbers are also worth reading carefully: a warm query inside the library is a map scan, but the CLI still pays for daemon IPC, serialization, and writing output. Full-output queries are not magic. Narrow queries are where the warm graph starts to feel like cheating, because it is no longer doing evaluation work to answer them. ↩ It concerns me so much in fact, that I have Nix cgrouped to limit how much CPU, RAM and IO it can use thanks to Systemd’s cgroup accounting. Without it, Nix evaluation regularly kills low-end machines that I happen to have the misfortune of rebuilding on. ↩ While implementing remote workers for Evix I spent an afternoon or two absolutely convinced that I had written a deadlock because the remote benchmark was catastrophically slower than the local one. I mean the numbers were off the charts. The program was fine. The socket was patiently batching tiny messages in exactly the way TCP was allowed to do. One little code review from a friend, one setsockopt, a little less dignity, and the numbers looked sane again. Oh joy. ↩

blocks.html_en: Most, if not all, Nix tools I build (or at least, consider building) eventually want to do one little, very boring thing. They want a list of derivations an expression produces, and well, they need to find a way to get it. Not necessarily a build log—I’ve got a crate for that already and those are relatively trivial to parse already and not a closure but a list of jobs. Those usually require their attribute paths, names, systems, .drv paths and outputs to be visible and if you’re building something like Hydra then you need those before you can decide what to build, i.e., those are the things a CI system needs before it can decide what changed. While I haven’t quite tried, those are also things I imagine a deployment tool needs before it can decide whether the graph in front of it is the same abomination or/and deployment abstraction it saw five minutes ago.

blocks.html_en: I think the first time I’ve used this model was in my NixOS configuration’s CI where I combined nix-eval-jobs with jq and then passed the graph to Nix to build my things. Important distinction here is that a CI system asks on every push. A fleet of nixosConfigurations asks once per host, then again when you only care about one system, then again when you want a proper diff. A watcher asks after each file write. A daemon asks because a separate command invocation forgot what the previous one already learned. And evaluating a real flake is not free either. It is thousands of attributes, lazy thunks waking up (just enough to hurt you), and a wall-clock cost you notice mostly because you pay it again for the next question. Now let me state the obvious: Nix’s eval cache sucks. And I can tell you that I am not interested in a cache-shaped thing that’s masquerading as one. Although Evix fixes that too. Just because.

blocks.html_en: Evix is what I wrote to solve my general woes around structured and persistent evaluations. It is a library-first async Nix evaluation engine that evaluates flakes, files or inline expressions through the stable Nix C API, via my very own nix-bindings, and reports derivations as typed events. There exists a CLI too, in case you want to replace nix-eval-jobs in your CI setups, but despite being very useful it is not the center of my design. The center is the embeddable library API and Session: a long-lived evaluation object that can stream the first run, retain the graph, answer queries, compute diffs, and watch local inputs for changes. The daemon is complementary, and it is ultimately just that idea moved behind a Unix socket so separate command invocations can share a warm session instead of re-enacting the fall of man every time you type a new command.

blocks.html_en: As much as I want to replace Nix, Evix is not a Nix replacement and I don’t replace Nix yet. Evix is, most simply put, the architecture around evaluation: process isolation, scheduling, backpressure, event accumulation, daemon state, remote workers, and enough respect for the C API that I do not have to scrape a terminal and call it data or torture myself with the C++ API. If there is a technical marvel here, it is not that I discovered fire. No, I was not there to discover fire (I’m not that old) but the parts of Evix are quite interesting nevertheless. Most of them mundane and sharp-edged, line up into a proper model where Nix evaluation becomes something more reliable and something you can pretty much hold on to—for the lack of a better term.

blocks.html_en: The model starts smaller than what you might expect. A worker does not walk a whole flake as most tools often do as I’ve come to observe. It evaluates one attribute path and returns one event. Hand it packages.x86_64-linux.hello and it navigates from the root value to that path through the Nix C API, auto-calling functions on the way when the configured arguments make that possible. Then it asks what it found. If the value is a derivation, Evix reads the derivation name, target system, .drv path and outputs. If requested, it also reads meta, input derivations from the .drv, Hydra-style constituents, and registers GC roots. If the value is an attribute set, Evix does not recursively disappear into it. It returns the child names as an event. If forcing the value throws, that is an error event. Nonfatal errors are part of the stream, not a reason to throw away the whole run.

blocks.html_en: It’s also worth talking about Evix’s benchmark suite. I’m yet to benchmark Evix in more advanced production scenarios, but on the current toy3 benchmark fixture, which is designed to measure scheduling and evaluation overhead rather than build time, Evix with one local worker sits around 318ms, four local workers around 198ms, and eight local workers around 216ms. nix-eval-jobs with four workers is around 359ms on the same fixture. Remote-only evaluation over loopback with four workers lands around 269ms. 4 Do not read those numbers as a universal law. The fixture is rather cheap, so overheads are loud and real flakes will move the constants around. Read them as evidence that the session, graph and distribution model are not bought with a throughput tax large enough to make the project silly.

blocks.html_en: After each attribute, the worker checks its maximum resident set size against a configured limit, 4 GB by default. If the worker is over the line, it returns a Restart status and exits. The coordinator goes ahead and spawns a fresh worker and continues feeding the same queue. The graph is in the parent, so the graph survives. The worker’s heap is in the worker, so the leak does not become some kind of a blood oath the host process has to honor forever. This is especially important if you’re interested in embedding. By default, local workers re-exec the embedding binary and enter the worker protocol when EVIX_WORKER is set. If your host program cannot or should not re-exec itself, you can point ConfigBuilder::worker_exe at a dedicated worker executable instead. The worker protocol is still the same: setup message, work path, event, status. The magic is mostly refusing to make the embedding process also be the place where libnix gets to leak memory for sport.

blocks.html_en: The first version of the idea that evolved to the Evix of today could be explained roughly as “evaluate once, keep the graph.” That is, well, still true, but the current model is more precise: an evaluation configuration opens a Session; the session streams the initial event log once; draining that stream populates warm state; queries and diffs operate on that warm state until you replace it. This sounds like API trivia, which I’d love to provide, but it is genuinely important because it basically changes the shape of the programs you can write. A CLI pipeline gives you a list. A session gives you memory and identity. The graph is a HashMap keyed by attribute path, with derivation records as values. A query is a filter over that graph: systems, attribute prefixes, exact attrs, names, .drv paths, include patterns, exclude patterns. A diff is a fresh evaluation compared with the previous graph; if the same attribute path points to a different .drv path, Evix treats it as a remove and an add. Something something the ship of Theseus something.

blocks.html_en: The daemon is a thin extension of the same idea as Evix. It listens on a Unix socket, keeps a small registry of warm sessions, and keys them by the evaluation config: input, arguments, Nix options, worker count, memory limit, remote endpoints, metadata flags, the whole boring lot. It’s also primed to do a lot more.

blocks.html_en: Each remote connection gets its own evaluator subprocess on the far end, so --remote builder-a:7357 x86_64-linux 4 means four worker connections to that endpoint. With --workers 0 and at least one remote, the coordinator can run no local workers at all. At that point your local process is almost pure scheduler: it owns the queue and graph, while the machines that can actually evaluate the interesting systems do the forcing. On this note, however, system routing has a subtle limitation: a derivation’s system is not known until the attribute has been evaluated. Evix therefore cannot always know, before evaluation, which machine is the perfect one for a path. Remotes declare the systems they own, and the coordinator checks returned derivations against the pool. If some local, catch-all, or owning remote accepts that system, the event is valid. If no worker in the pool accepts it, evaluation fails by name with a fatal error instead of quietly losing the derivation. That is less magical than perfect pre-routing and much better than lying to ourselves or making a best-effort guess.

blocks.html_en: There is also a store-directory handshake. blocks.html_en: Earlier in this post I’ve mentioned using Nix (and friends) in CI. If you don’t remember this, it’s fine—I’m aware I’ve been yapping for too long. Long story short, this entire endeavour—as expected from all the context and pain surrounding GHA— was done using Bash. blocks.html_en: That is also why the project is not really about the CLI. The CLI is convenient, and I use it, but the library is the point. blocks.html_en: What Evix Solves

sentences.en: What Evix Solves
sentences.zh: Evix 解决什么问题

blocks.html_en: The problem Evix solves is not “Nix evaluation exists.” The problem is that serious tools around Nix need evaluation to become a reusable service boundary, and not a ceremony performed by a subprocess every time. For CI specifically, the useful object is a graph that can be diffed between commits. For your fleet of NixOS configurations, it is a graph that can be filtered by system, prefix, name or .drv path. For a watch command, it is a previous graph and a new graph with errors attached to the comparison instead of hidden in a terminal scrollback. For distributed evaluation, it is a queue of independent attribute paths that local and remote workers can pull from without changing what the final graph means. For an embedding application, it is a typed API that does not ask the caller to summon a shell and interpret stdout as ontology. Thus, this I’ve built Evix. Circus needs to evaluate jobsets often, keep them around, ask what changed, and eventually hand builds to the right place. I do not want that CI to spend its life recomputing the same graph because the previous process threw away the one thing I cared about. I do not want an aarch64 board to be represented by an x86_64 laptop. I do not want one broken package to make the rest of the job graph unknowable. I do not want the evaluator and the builder to become one swollen process just because both words appear near each other in a README. Yada yada. My point is that Evix draws the line where I needed it. Evaluation discovers derivations. Building is somebody else’s problem, usually Nix itself or Circus. Building is stateful, resource-hungry, cache-sensitive, failure-prone in completely different ways, and full of policy. Evaluation is already enough of a problem, and I have 99 problems. Evaluation is 99 of them.

blocks.html_en: Where It Stops

sentences.en: Where It Stops
sentences.zh: 停在哪里

blocks.html_en: Evix is rather young, and there are real ceilings. If you end up trying Evix and get rather disappointed, I ask that you attribute to its lack of maturity. I’ve recently released 2.0.0 to revise its model in its entirety and it was a much larger refactor than I feel I was equipped to deal with. Still, it turned out quite well and Circus’ own CI test suite is now green across the board. That said, I’ll be remiss if I don’t mention the issues such as that a worker can still die inside one awful force. Remote workers need compatible stores and trusted networking; expose the TCP service over a tunnel or VPN, not to the entire internet like you are trying to speedrun regret. System routing is also rather constrained by the fact that the system is discovered after evaluation—rather unsurprisingly. The daemon keeps warm sessions, but it is not a distributed database and should not be asked to cosplay as one. THOUGH, it may be possible in the future. Last but not least, remember that the C API is stable enough to build on, but Nix is still Nix, with all the fun that implies and several other kinds of fun it invents at runtime.

blocks.html_en: There are also things Evix intentionally does not do. One big example is building. I’ve considered giving it a component like evix build, but compared to the surface of evaluation, building is truly a different kind of monster. To let Evix also do building, I would be required to solve several problems that are not even remotely addressed in flakes, and I do not have the patience for that can of worms yet—no, I’m not a patient man.

blocks.html_en: It does not solve binary cache policy. It does not make remote flakes locally watchable when there is no local path to subscribe to. It does not turn a Nix graph into a web frontend by itself. It will tell you what derivations exist, what paths they would produce, what inputs they mention if you ask, and how a later evaluation differs from an earlier one. That is the promise. A narrow promise, but a useful one. I do not expect Evix to be groundbreaking, but I expect it to be useful. It’s got a lot of potential, and thus my dear reader, I invite you to harness it. Come talk to me, let me know what you need even.

blocks.html_en: So, that is Evix as it stands today. It’s certainly been through a lot of iterations over I can probably only describe as ages before I decided to sit down and port my low-effort Python/Bash/C++ bullshit to proper Rust. It is not a one-shot evaluator (anymore) with a nicer coat of paint, but a session-oriented evaluation engine with a proper CLI attached. The combination changes the question from “how do I print the jobs again?” to “what do I want to ask the graph I already have?” If you’re building with Evix it gives you a very nice toolkit to answer your questions in mere seconds. Evix, however, tries to make it an object: scheduled, isolated, queryable, diffable, and capable of crossing machine boundaries without pretending those boundaries are not there.

content_html_zh:
我构建（或者至少考虑构建）的大多数（如果不是全部）Nix 工具最终都想做一件非常无聊的小事。 他们想要一个表达式产生的派生列表，而且他们需要找到一种方法来获得它。 不一定是构建日志——我已经有一个板条箱了，解析这些日志已经相对简单，而且不是一个闭包，而是一个作业列表。 这些通常要求它们的属性路径、名称、系统、.drv 路径和输出可见，如果您正在构建像 Hydra 这样的东西，那么您需要这些，然后才能决定构建什么，也就是说，这些是 CI 系统在决定更改内容之前需要的东西。 虽然我还没有完全尝试过，但我认为部署工具在决定其前面的图表是否与五分钟前看到的相同的令人厌恶的或/和部署抽象之前需要这些东西。

这不完全是一个问题陈述，但这或多或少是我遇到的问题。 然而，因为这听起来像是一次性成本，但您最终会意识到事实并非如此。 您还意识到这与内部循环有关。 如果你没有意识到它的含义，那么你就会犯我犯过的同样的错误，并思考你自己是多么的聪明，以及你如何完全、绝对地通过一遍又一遍地重复使用相同的技巧而逃脱惩罚。

我想我第一次使用这个模型是在我的 NixOS 配置的 CI 中，我将 nix-eval-jobs 与 jq 结合起来，然后将图表传递给 Nix 来构建我的东西。 这里的重要区别是 CI 系统在每次推送时都会询问。 一组 nixosConfigurations 对每个主机询问一次，然后当您只关心一个系统时询问一次，然后当您需要适当的差异时询问一次。 每次文件写入后，观察者都会询问。 守护进程询问是因为单独的命令调用忘记了前一个命令已经学到的内容。 评估真正的薄片也不是免费的。 这是数以千计的属性，懒惰的重击声醒来（足以伤害你），以及你注意到的挂钟成本，主要是因为你为下一个问题再次支付了它。 现在让我陈述一个显而易见的事实：Nix 的 eval 缓存很糟糕。 我可以告诉你，我对伪装成缓存形状的东西不感兴趣。 尽管 Evix 也解决了这个问题。 只是因为。

很长一段时间以来，我一直认为我的抱怨是评估速度很慢（确实如此）并且输出解析起来很烦人（确实如此）。 这与晚上散步时整架钢琴掉落在头顶上的体验大致相同，但这并不是破坏我这一天的原因。 最让我恼火的是，并不是有一架受重力挑战的钢琴决定破坏我晚上的散步，而是进行评估的程序已经构建了有趣的结构，打印了它的表示，然后死掉了。 自然地，图表也会随之消失。 去算算吧。

当我开始调用 jq（我不是它的忠实粉丝）时，我慢慢开始怀疑我正在使用的工具是...... 错误的。 正如我所提到的，我最初是通过在我的问题上使用 nix-eval-jobs 来开始的，我不想让你认为这是一个糟糕的软件，1 但它几乎不是我想要的。 仍然有很多令人烦恼的空白，通过传统方式需要很长时间才能填补，而且我知道这样做很糟糕，因为 C++ 很糟糕。 不管怎样，我的观点是，它是一个相对较好的工具，可以找到 Nix 工作评估员应该找到的东西，并且 Evix 在基准测试中仍然依赖它，因为我承认这一点，并且我努力创造比它更好的东西。

输入，埃维克斯

我写 Evix 是为了解决我在结构化和持久评估方面的普遍问题。 它是一个库优先的异步 Nix 评估引擎，通过稳定的 Nix C API、我自己的 nix 绑定来评估薄片、文件或内联表达式，并将派生报告为类型化事件。 也存在一个 CLI，以防您想在 CI 设置中替换 nix-eval-jobs，但尽管它非常有用，但它不是我设计的中心。 中心是可嵌入库 API 和会话：一个长期存在的评估对象，可以流式传输第一次运行、保留图形、回答查询、计算差异并观察本地输入的更改。 守护进程是互补的，最终只是将这个想法转移到了 Unix 套接字之后，因此单独的命令调用可以共享一个热会话，而不是每次键入新命令时都重新上演人类的堕落。

尽管我很想取代 Nix，但 Evix 并不是 Nix 的替代品，而且我还不会取代 Nix。 最简单地说，Evix 是围绕评估的架构：进程隔离、调度、背压、事件累积、守护进程状态、远程工作人员以及对 C API 的足够尊重，我不必抓取终端并将其称为数据或用 C++ API 折磨自己。 如果说这里有什么技术奇迹的话，那就不是我发现了火。 不，我不是来发现火的（我没那么老），但 Evix 的各个部分仍然非常有趣。 它们中的大多数都是平凡而尖锐的，排列成一个适当的模型，在这个模型中，Nix 评估变得更可靠，并且你几乎可以坚持——因为缺乏更好的术语。

一种价值，一种事件

如果你还没有厌倦我，我想向你描述一下这个模型。 也许你会发现它很有趣，或者也许你有比我更好的想法，你会帮助开发我的。 无论哪种情况，我都想用这篇文章的其余部分来讨论 Evix 的运作方式。

该模型一开始比您预期的要小。 正如我所观察到的，工人不会像大多数工具经常做的那样走完整个薄片。 它评估一个属性路径并返回一个事件。 将其交给packages.x86_64-linux.hello，它会通过Nix C API从根值导航到该路径，当配置的参数使之成为可能时，会自动调用函数。 然后它会询问发现了什么。 如果该值是派生，Evix 会读取派生名称、目标系统、.drv 路径并输出。 如果需要，它还会读取元、来自 .drv 的输入派生、Hydra 风格的成分，并注册 GC 根。 如果该值是一个属性集，Evix 不会递归地消失在其中。 它将孩子的名字作为事件返回。 如果强制该值抛出，那就是一个错误事件。 非致命错误是流的一部分，而不是放弃整个运行的原因。

最后一句话比看起来更重要。 大型尼克斯图并不是维多利亚时代或 19 世纪奥斯曼帝国的小说，其中每个角色都必须生存到最后一章。 一个坏包不应该删除它旁边的包。 错误需要名称、路径和足够的结构，以便调用者（以及您）可以决定如何处理它们。 字节流可以告诉您出了什么问题。 键入的事件可以告诉您哪里出了问题，并且仍然让图表的其余部分到达。 每个人都赢了！

看到 Evix 正在行走的东西会有所帮助。 片状输出通常是一棵属性集树，其叶子处有派生，修剪成如下所示：

.#                       root; always recursed into
├─ packages
│  ├─ x86_64-linux       attrset    (expand: one work item per child)
│  │  ├─ hello           derivation (leaf)  hello-2.12.1
│  │  ├─ git             derivation (leaf)  git-2.45.2
│  │  └─ ripgrep         derivation (leaf)  ripgrep-14.1.0
│  └─ aarch64-linux      attrset
│     ├─ hello           derivation (leaf)
│     └─ firefox         derivation (leaf)
└─ devShells
   └─ x86_64-linux
      └─ default         derivation (leaf)

看看我的艺术才华吧！ 递归并不存在于一个工作人员拥有的调用堆栈内。 它位于队列中。 协调器使用根路径为队列播种。 工作人员拉出一条路径，对其进行评估，然后返回一个事件。 attrset 事件向队列添加更多路径。 派生事件是终结的。 错误事件是该路径的终点。 当队列为空并且没有工作人员忙碌时，运行结束。

作为队列而不是私有递归，该树大致如下所示，无论工作人员碰巧回答什么顺序：

queue: [ .# ]
  .#                            attrset    -> enqueue packages, devShells
  packages                      attrset    -> enqueue packages.x86_64-linux, ...
  packages.x86_64-linux         attrset    -> enqueue ...hello, ...git, ...ripgrep
  packages.x86_64-linux.hello   derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing
  packages.x86_64-linux.git     derivation -> emit; enqueue nothing
  ...
empty queue, nothing in flight  -> we're done
[!NOTE] 默认情况下，Evix 不会递归到每个属性集。 它遵循与此类工具通常遵循的相同基本思想：在根处递归，并递归到选择使用 recurseForDerivations 的 attrsets。 当你确实想要踢掉每一扇门时，有一个 --force-recurse 选项，但默认选项不那么愚蠢。 Nixpkgs 有很多房间。 有些包含就业机会。 有些包含机械。 有些包含一些让你后悔好奇作为一个概念并思考可怜的猫的东西。

重要的不变量（我称之为重要的，因为它导致了许多破坏和很多痛苦）是，答案是一个由属性路径键控的图，而不是由事件发生到达的顺序键控。 一名工人和四名工人应生成相同的图表。 当然，本地工人和远程工人应该为同一个蓄电池供电。 事件流是临时的，因为程序实时存在，但结果图不应该依赖于调度程序的运气。 这是使用并行性的许可。 2

还值得一提的是 Evix 的基准测试套件。 我还没有在更高级的生产场景中对 Evix 进行基准测试，但在当前的 toy3 基准测试装置（旨在测量调度和评估开销而不是构建时间）上，具有一名本地工人的 Evix 约为 318 毫秒，四名本地工人约为 198 毫秒，八名本地工人约为 216 毫秒。 在同一装置上，有四个工作人员的 nix-eval-jobs 大约需要 359 毫秒。 四个工作人员对环回进行仅远程评估大约需要 269 毫秒。 4 不要将这些数字视为普遍法则。 该装置相当便宜，因此开销很大，并且真正的雪花会使常数发生变化。 将它们视为证据，表明会话、图表和分发模型不是用大到足以使该项目变得愚蠢的吞吐量税购买的。

进程，而不是线程

如果您曾经目睹过 Nix 评估超出了您的记忆范围，并在完成四分之三的过程中被杀死，整个运行过程也随之结束，这就是您所关心的部分。 5 Evix 工作线程是子进程，而不是线程。 主机进程拥有队列和暖图。 每个工作线程都拥有其 Nix 上下文、存储句柄、评估状态和根值。 这个边界就像 Unix 一样是粗糙的，也就是说，它是计算中为数不多的仍然有效的粗糙事物之一。 对此我也有一些粗俗的话要说。

在每个属性之后，工作线程会根据配置的限制（默认情况下为 4 GB）检查其最大驻留集大小。 如果工作线程越线，它将返回重新启动状态并退出。 协调器继续生成一个新的工作人员，并继续为同一队列提供数据。 该图位于父级中，因此该图仍然存在。 工作线程的堆位于工作线程中，因此泄漏不会成为主机进程必须永远遵守的某种血誓。 如果您对嵌入感兴趣，这一点尤其重要。 默认情况下，本地工作程序会在设置 EVIX_WORKER 时重新执行嵌入二进制文件并输入工作程序协议。 如果您的主机程序不能或不应该重新执行自身，您可以将 ConfigBuilder::worker_exe 指向专用的工作可执行文件。 工作协议仍然相同：设置消息、工作路径、事件、状态。 神奇之处在于拒绝让嵌入过程也成为 libnix 泄漏内存以进行运动的地方。

在结束本节之前，值得保留的一个脚注是内存检查发生在属性之间。 它捕捉到了工人在多条路径上生长的常见情况，但是，它并不能避免一个属性在控制返回检查之前引爆中力。 Evix 可以使某个项目超时、中止工作进程并重新连接。 它可以报告 stderr。 它可以让宿主活下去。 它不能使 libnix 中断进入它不具有的属性。 我是一个穷人。 我所拥有的只是一个进程边界和一个 RSS 检查。 估计预算不同吧

会议就是产品

这个想法的第一个版本演变成了今天的 Evix，可以粗略地解释为“评估一次，保留图表”。 这仍然是正确的，但当前的模型更加精确：评估配置打开一个会话；会话流式传输初始事件日志一次；排空该流填充的温暖状态；查询和差异在该热状态下运行，直到您替换它为止。 这听起来像是我很乐意提供的 API 琐事，但它确实很重要，因为它基本上改变了您可以编写的程序的形式。 CLI 管道为您提供了一个列表。 会话给你记忆和身份。 该图是一个以属性路径为键的 HashMap，以派生记录作为值。 查询是对该图的过滤器：系统、属性前缀、精确属性、名称、.drv 路径、包含模式、排除模式。 diff 是与之前的图表相比的新评估；如果相同的属性路径指向不同的 .drv 路径，Evix 会将其视为删除和添加。 某事某事忒修斯之船某事。

库 API 更直接地公开了这一点。 Session::stream 是一次性的，因为初始评估是一次性的。 Session::query_snapshot 读取暖图。 Session::diff_once 重新评估并在新图中交换。 Session::watch 在本地文件和本地薄片输入的 fs 通知之后执行相同的小舞蹈。 有界变体的存在是因为嵌入器有时需要背压，而无界通道是将“我的标准输出很慢”变成“亲爱的，为什么我的进程如此巨大？”的好方法。 问我怎么知道的。 事实上，请不要。

守护进程（主机）

该守护进程是与 Evix 相同想法的精简扩展。 它监听 Unix 套接字，保留一个小型的热会话注册表，并通过评估配置对它们进行键控：输入、参数、Nix 选项、工作线程数、内存限制、远程端点、元数据标志，以及所有无聊的东西。 它还准备做更多事情。

实际上，守护进程的想法来自于我们在 Circus 中的目标，即不仅分发构建，还分发评估。 忽略配置的缓存不是缓存，它是延迟良好的骗子。 如果您使用一组覆盖进行评估并使用另一组覆盖进行查询，您应该得到一个未命中的结果，而不是一个漂亮快速的错误答案。 同样，如果一个缓存不是根据不同机器的缓存，那么它就不是一个正确的缓存。

除了守护进程之外，还存在一些其他 evix 命令来包装 Evix 优秀的（如果我可以自己这么说的话）库接口：

  • evix eval 评估一次并传输 NDJSON。 如果守护进程可用，它也可以留下一个热会话。
  • evix 查询向已经热的守护进程会话请求过滤后的快照。
  • evix diff 重新评估并与暖图进行比较。
  • evix watch 评估本地文件或 flake 并在观察的输入变化时发出差异。
  • evix worker 启动远程工作者服务。
  • 如果您不希望 CLI 假装所有这一切都是由神圣干预发生的，则 evix 守护程序会显式启动 Unix 套接字守护程序。

所以我的观点是，Evix 不仅仅是打印相同列表的更快方法。 这是一种使评估图保持足够长的时间的方法，以便后续问题成为普通的程序操作。 它也不是 Nix 评估包装器。 Evix 是专门为 Circus 设计的，这是我在 Manic Systems 开发的 CI（希望能够面向未来），其中“等待评估”和“询问已经评估的世界发生了什么变化”之间的区别对于我们的用例至关重要。 后者对于住在里面来说是一个更好的句子——这也是做九头蛇所做的事情的更好的方式，而且也更可靠。

不在这里的工人（他们正在罢工）

工作人员是一个奇怪的小东西，我决定从 Circus 的分布式代理设计/概念中反映出来，其中工作人员接收属性路径并返回事件。 一旦你这样表达，就没有什么深层次的理由它必须与协调器在同一台机器上——类似于 Circus 的代理。 这就是 Evix 不再是本地优化而开始看起来像老式意义上的调度程序的地方。 它有一个队列，以及关于谁应该做什么的意见。 远程工作人员是使用 Cap’n Proto 消息的 TCP 服务。 还记得我说过分布式评估吗？ 是的，就是这样。

连接打开并进行设置握手，其中包含评估配置、协议版本、令牌和预期存储目录。 然后它重复这个小循环：工作（路径）消失，事件和状态回来。 设置 TCP_NODELAY 是因为该协议是每个属性一个微小的请求响应，而 Nagle 算法是当网络堆栈决定您的延迟配置文件应该成为道德教训时发生的情况。 6

每个远程连接在远端都有自己的评估器子进程，因此 --remote builder-a:7357 x86_64-linux 4 意味着到该端点的四个工作连接。 使用 --workers 0 和至少一个远程工作人员，协调器根本无法运行任何本地工作人员。 那时，您的本地进程几乎是纯粹的调度程序：它拥有队列和图形，而可以实际评估有趣系统的机器则执行强制操作。 然而，在这一点上，系统路由有一个微妙的限制：在评估属性之前，派生的系统是未知的。 因此，在评估之前，Evix 并不总是知道哪台机器最适合一条路径。 远程节点声明他们拥有的系统，协调器根据池检查返回的派生。 如果某个本地的、包罗万象的或拥有的远程设备接受该系统，则该事件有效。 如果池中没有工作人员接受它，则评估会因名称而失败并出现致命错误，而不是悄悄地丢失推导。 这不像完美的预路由那么神奇，但比欺骗自己或尽力猜测要好得多。

还有一个存储目录握手。 Nix 存储目录与协调器的存储目录不匹配的远程会被拒绝，因为 .drv 和输出路径只有在指向相同类型的存储时才对使用者有意义。 这不是远程建筑。 明显地。 Evix 并没有复制构建产品。 它正在评估和报告推导。 如果你想要远程构建输出传输，那属于 Nix 的构建器模型或 evix 之上的 CI 系统，而不是假装它长大后也想成为构建器的评估器。 坦白说，这是我最喜欢Evix的部分，因为它并不宏伟。 它并没有说“分布式系统”，然后要求控制平面、服务网格，甚至更糟…… YAML。 它表示工作单元已经是可序列化的，事件已经是可序列化的，并且工作人员已经是一次性的。 在它们之间放置一个插座。 使协议明确。 拒绝不能表示相同商店路径的遥控器。 继续前行。

在没有定制 Bash 的情况下与 Nix 交谈

在这篇文章的前面，我提到过在 CI 中使用 Nix（和朋友）。 如果你不记得了，那也没关系——我知道我已经嚷嚷太久了。 长话短说，正如从 GHA 的所有背景和痛苦中所预期的那样，整个工作都是使用 Bash 完成的。 也就是说，在不调用 nix eval 或 C++ API 的情况下执行 Nix 评估通常不太容易。 在这里我想提一下 Evix 的另一个“安静”部分。 如前所述，Evix 通过 C API 与 Nix 对话。 这样做并不是为了美观纯粹，尽管我确实喜欢不像动物一样解析面向人类的文本（或使用 C++）。 这样做是因为嵌入库需要类型边界。

输入是以下三项之一：

  1. 片状参考，
  2. Nix 文件，或者
  3. 内联表达式。

自动调用参数可以是表达式或字符串。 锁定时可以覆盖薄片输入。 在工作线程打开存储或构建其评估状态之前，Nix 选项可以传递到工作线程环境。 Flake 锁定是在 Worker 启动之前处理的，并且锁定的图会导入到 Worker 内部，因此多 Worker 评估并不是每个进程都针对当时 Flake 的含义发明自己的答案。 本地路径 flake 会根据其 flake.lock 检查；非本地裁判仍然是一个需要注意可重复性的地方，因为现实仍然是粗鲁的。

首先输入输出，然后输入 JSON。 Rust 枚举具有派生、属性集和错误的变体。 CLI 将它们扁平化为 NDJSON，因为 NDJSON 有用但无聊，这是我非常尊重格式的两个属性。 使用 --meta，Evix 尝试将元转换为自由格式的 JSON，并删除无法强制或表示的嵌套字段。 使用 --show-input-drvs，它从 .drv 文件读取输入派生。 选民的就业总量也包含这些。 这些都不需要正则表达式或复数，遗憾。

这也是为什么该项目并不是真正关于 CLI 的。 CLI 很方便，我也使用它，但库才是重点。 Rust 服务可以打开会话、排出流、查询热图、计算差异或运行观察程序，而无需从文本中剔除和重建结构。 如果服务是 Web 后端，Evix 可以作为您真正想要的任何 HTTP 或 WebSocket API 背后的本机 sidecar 或守护程序。 如果您想要浏览器 WASM，坏消息是：当前后端是原生设计的。 它链接 libnix，打开 Nix 存储，使用 Unix 子进程，并使用 Unix 套接字和 TCP。 浏览器内评估器需要不同的后端，可能是我们完全控制的后端。 悲伤，我知道。 唉，这就是我们所拥有的。 但这还不是结束。

Evix 解决什么问题

Evix 解决的问题不是“Nix 评估存在”。 问题在于 Nix 周围的重要工具需要评估才能成为可重用的服务边界，而不是每次都由子流程执行的仪式。 特别是对于 CI，有用的对象是一个可以在提交之间进行区分的图。 对于您的 NixOS 配置群，它是一个可以按系统、前缀、名称或 .drv 路径进行过滤的图表。 对于监视命令，它是一个先前的图表和一个新的图表，其中的错误附加到比较中，而不是隐藏在终端回滚中。 对于分布式评估，它是本地和远程工作人员可以从中提取独立属性路径的队列，而无需更改最终图形的含义。 对于嵌入应用程序来说，它是一个类型化 API，不会要求调用者调用 shell 并将 stdout 解释为本体。 因此，我构建了 Evix。 Circus 需要经常评估工作集，保留它们，询问发生了什么变化，并最终手工构建到正确的位置。 我不希望 CI 一生都在重新计算同一个图，因为之前的过程抛弃了我关心的一件事。 我不希望 aarch64 板由 x86_64 笔记本电脑代表。 我不希望一个破损的包裹使作业图的其余部分变得不可知。 我不希望评估者和构建者仅仅因为两个词在自述文件中出现得很接近而成为一个臃肿的过程。 雅达雅达。 我的观点是，Evix 在我需要的地方画了线。 评估发现推导。 建造是别人的问题，通常是尼克斯本身或马戏团的问题。 构建是有状态的、资源匮乏的、缓存敏感的、以完全不同的方式容易失败并且充满策略的。 评价已经够问题了，我有99个问题。 评价为99分。

停在哪里

Evix还很年轻，而且还有真正的天花板。 如果您最终尝试了 Evix 并感到相当失望，我要求您将其归咎于它不够成熟。 我最近发布了 2.0.0 来全面修改其模型，这是一个比我认为我有能力处理的更大的重构。 尽管如此，结果还是相当不错，Circus 自己的 CI 测试套件现在全面绿化。 也就是说，如果我不提及诸如工人仍然可能在可怕的力量中死亡之类的问题，那就是我的失职。 远程工作人员需要兼容的商店和可信的网络；通过隧道或 VPN 公开 TCP 服务，而不是像您试图快速运行后悔那样向整个互联网公开。 系统路由也受到系统是在评估后发现这一事实的限制——这并不奇怪。 该守护进程保持热会话，但它不是一个分布式数据库，不应该被要求扮演一个数据库。 不过，这在未来可能是可能的。 最后但并非最不重要的一点是，请记住，C API 足够稳定，可以在其基础上进行构建，但 Nix 仍然是 Nix，拥有它所暗示的所有乐趣以及它在运行时发明的其他几种乐趣。

还有一些事情 Evix 故意不做。 一个重要的例子就是建筑。 我曾考虑过给它一个像 evix build 这样的组件，但与评估的表面相比，build 确实是一种不同的怪物。 为了让 Evix 也能进行建造，我需要解决几个远距离解决的问题，而我还没有耐心对待那堆蠕虫——不，我不是一个有耐心的人。

它不解决二进制缓存策略。 当没有本地路径可供订阅时，它不会使远程薄片在本地可观看。 它本身不会将 Nix 图转变为 Web 前端。 它将告诉您存在哪些派生，它们会产生哪些路径，如果您询问，它们会提到哪些输入，以及后来的评估与之前的评估有何不同。 这就是承诺。 这是一个狭隘的承诺，但却是一个有用的承诺。 我并不期望 Evix 具有开创性，但我希望它有用。 它有很大的潜力，因此我亲爱的读者，我邀请您利用它。 来跟我谈谈，让我知道你需要什么。

结束语

这就是今天的 Evix。 在我决定坐下来将我的省力 Python/Bash/C++ 废话移植到正确的 Rust 之前，它确实经历了很多迭代，我可能只能描述为好几年了。 它不再是一个具有更好油漆涂层的一次性评估器，而是一个带有适当 CLI 的面向会话的评估引擎。 这种组合改变了“如何再次打印作业？”的问题。 到“我想问我已有的图表什么？” 如果您使用 Evix 进行构建，它会为您提供一个非常好的工具包，可以在几秒钟内回答您的问题。 这就是我的“技巧”。 我想继续讲一点哲学，并说工具在一定程度上是由它让你记住的东西来定义的。 旧的形状使评估成为一项活动。 然而，Evix 试图使其成为一个对象：计划的、隔离的、可查询的、可比较的，并且能够跨越机器边界，而不假装这些边界不存在。

如果您只需要一个通过管道传输到 jq 的一次性列表，或者更确切地说，您只需要坚持，那么您不需要任何这些。 但无论如何，使用更简单的东西，享受罕见的奢侈，不需要我的问题。 我需要评估才能在程序中保持活力，使用类型值而不是字节流，并有足够的调度机制，使工作能够在大图、泄漏工作人员和不在我手下的机器中幸存下来。 这是一个狭隘的需求，也是我的需求。

如果这听起来也像你的问题，Evix 在 GitHub 上。 干杯。
